cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: ACLY is a homotetrameric citrate lyase that cleaves citrate into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate, serving as the principal bridge between mitochondrial TCA-cycle metabolism and cytosolic/nuclear acetyl-CoA pools required for de novo lipogenesis, cholesterol biosynthesis, protein acetylation, and chromatin remodeling. In the cytosol, ACLY-derived acetyl-CoA sustains fatty acid synthesis and regulates ferroptosis susceptibility by maintaining FSP1 acetylation at K168, preventing its ubiquitin-dependent degradation [PMID:39881208]; its activity is stimulated by AKT-mediated S455 phosphorylation and Lyn-mediated tyrosine phosphorylation, and attenuated by multiple E3 ligase-dependent degradation routes (CUL3-KLHL25, Hrd1/ERAD, NEDD4, and SQSTM1/p62-mediated selective autophagy) as well as SIRT2-dependent deacetylation [PMID:27664236, PMID:32888949, PMID:35404187, PMID:38426936]. In the nucleus, ACLY translocates in response to DNA damage (ATM/AKT) or ischemia-reperfusion and supplies acetyl-CoA for histone acetylation that directs DNA repair pathway choice toward homologous recombination, controls inflammatory and immune gene programs in macrophages and T cells, and regulates hepatoprotective transcription [PMID:28689661, PMID:37983829, PMID:39150482]. ACLY loss in CD8+ T cells triggers a compensatory ACSS2-dependent acetate pathway that partially sustains histone acetylation and chromatin accessibility at effector loci, and hyperactivation of ACLY by pathogenic α-synuclein drives mTORC1-dependent autophagy impairment in Parkinson's disease neuronal models [PMID:39150482, PMID:40262613].

ARIH1 (HHARI) is a RING-between-RING (RBR) E3 ubiquitin ligase that functions as a central effector of CRL-coupled ubiquitination and innate immune signaling. Its RING1 domain recruits the E2 enzyme UbcH7 and uses a unique Zn²⁺-loop II steric wedge to enforce an open E2~Ub conformation, directing ubiquitin transfer through an obligate thioester intermediate on the RING2 catalytic cysteine — a RING/HECT hybrid mechanism capable of forming both lysine isopeptide and serine oxyester bonds on substrates [PMID:21532592, PMID:28552575, PMID:37870100]. Auto-inhibited in isolation, ARIH1 is allosterically activated by association with neddylated Cullin-RING ligase complexes, whereupon it ubiquitinates diverse substrates including PD-L1 (primed by GSK3α phosphorylation), DNA-PKcs, 4EHP, cGAS (via ISGylation), HER2, and MFN2, thereby controlling immune checkpoint protein turnover, DNA damage-induced translational arrest, cGAS-STING pathway activation, and mitochondrial dynamics [PMID:24076655, PMID:33879767, PMID:25624349, PMID:36217001, PMID:37429863]. ARIH1 also mono-ISGylates cGAS at Lys187 to promote its oligomerization and type I interferon production, and ARIH1 knockout mice show hypersensitivity to HSV-1 and altered autoimmune responses [PMID:36217001].

BTBD9 is a substrate-recognition adaptor of the CUL3-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase complex that ubiquitylates and degrades specific substrates to regulate cell migration, synaptic function, dopaminergic signaling, and motor behavior. As part of the CRL3 complex, BTBD9 targets TNFAIP1 for polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, suppressing cancer cell migration [PMID:32327643], and promotes ubiquitination of IMPDH2 in a neuronal cell context linked to sleep homeostasis [PMID:35449961]. In neurons, BTBD9 modulates synaptic plasticity, dopamine receptor expression, and potassium channel currents in cerebellar Purkinje cells, with loss of Btbd9 enhancing hippocampal LTP, altering striatal D1/D2 receptor balance, and disrupting BK/SK channel activity leading to motor coordination deficits [PMID:22536397, PMID:32468214, PMID:36244636]. BTBD9 additionally engages the insulin/IGF-1–FOXO signaling axis, upregulating FOXO and decreasing AKT to confer neuroprotection against oxidative stress in dopaminergic neurons [PMID:35134179].

BTF3 is a general transcription factor that associates with RNA polymerase II and regulates expression of diverse target genes, thereby influencing DNA replication, cell survival, stem cell-like properties, and metabolic reprogramming across multiple cell types. The longer BTF3a isoform is transcriptionally active whereas the shorter BTF3b splice variant retains RNA pol II binding but lacks transcriptional activity, yet BTF3b specifically drives RFC subunit gene expression required for DNA replication and repair [PMID:2320128, PMID:33414468]. Beyond direct transcriptional control of targets including ESR1, FOXM1, CHD1L, PDCD2L, and RRAGD [PMID:30315845, PMID:37382415, PMID:33644029, PMID:40651979], BTF3 stabilizes the Polycomb protein BMI1, suppressing interferon signaling and promoting cancer stem-like self-renewal [PMID:31138311, PMID:33383560], and forms a complex with STAT3 to enhance its phosphorylation [PMID:36641250]. BTF3 is essential for postimplantation mouse development, with homozygous null embryos dying around embryonic day 6.5 [PMID:7655515].

CAND1 is a HEAT-repeat protein that functions as a substrate receptor exchange factor for cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases (CRLs), enabling the shared cullin-RBX1 scaffold to sample the full repertoire of F-box, BTB, and DCAF adaptor proteins. CAND1 selectively binds unneddylated cullins (CUL1–CUL4, CUL7), sterically occluding both the SKP1/adaptor-binding site via a β-hairpin insertion and the NEDD8-conjugation lysine, thereby accelerating dissociation of pre-existing substrate receptor modules by approximately one-million-fold and catalyzing their replacement [PMID:12504025, PMID:15537541, PMID:23453757, PMID:37339624]. Cullin neddylation displaces CAND1 and locks the active ligase configuration, while CSN-mediated deneddylation resets the cycle; CAND1 itself facilitates deneddylation and, on CRL2, preferentially accelerates complex disassembly over assembly, providing a selectivity filter for substrate degradation [PMID:16036220, PMID:38177676, PMID:41864201]. Through this exchange cycle CAND1 controls the turnover of diverse CRL substrates including p27 via SCF-Skp2, Nrf2 via CRL3-Keap1, calcineurin via SCF-atrogin1, Mob1b via SCF-FBXW11, ACAA2 via SCF-FBXO42, and HER2 via CRL7, thereby influencing cell-cycle progression, adipogenesis, cardiac hypertrophy, heart regeneration, hepatic lipid metabolism, and interferon signaling [PMID:16449638, PMID:23328082, PMID:35661710, PMID:40555744, PMID:37528093, PMID:41310794].

CPSF7 (CFIm59) is a large subunit of the cleavage factor Im (CFIm) complex that regulates mRNA 3′ end processing and alternative polyadenylation (APA), thereby controlling 3′ UTR length across the transcriptome. Within the CFIm heterotetramer, CPSF7 activates enhancer-containing poly(A) sites through its arginine-serine (RS) domain, which binds the Fip1 subunit of CPSF in a phosphorylation-regulated manner; genome-wide loss-of-function studies reveal that CPSF7 and its paralog CFIm68 exert distinct and sometimes opposing effects on poly(A) site selection [PMID:29276085, PMID:35993810]. Beyond canonical polyadenylation, the RS domain of CPSF7 participates in CFIm-mediated promotion of MAT2A detained intron splicing, linking the complex to S-adenosylmethionine homeostasis [PMID:33949310]. CPSF7-dependent APA of specific transcripts such as WWP2 and PTEN connects its RNA-processing activity to PI3K/AKT signaling output in liver and lung cancer cells [PMID:31837982, PMID:35993810].

CUL3 is a scaffold cullin protein that assembles with RBX1/ROC1 RING-finger protein and a large, diverse family of BTB-domain-containing substrate adaptors to form Cullin-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase (CRL3) complexes that ubiquitinate specific substrates for proteasomal degradation or non-degradative signaling. BTB-domain proteins such as KEAP1, SPOP, KLHL3, KLHL9/13, KLHL20, KLHL21, and KLHL25 each serve as exchangeable substrate-recognition modules that bridge CUL3 to distinct targets—including NRF2 (oxidative stress response), Aurora B (mitotic chromosome-to-midzone translocation and cytokinesis), WNK kinases (renal ion homeostasis), ULK1/Beclin-1 (autophagy termination), cyclin E (cell cycle control), ACLY (fatty acid metabolism), eIF4G1 (cap-dependent translation in neurons), and GluR6/GLR-1 (synaptic glutamate receptor turnover)—thereby governing an exceptionally broad substrate repertoire [PMID:13679922, PMID:15572695, PMID:17543862, PMID:26687681, PMID:23387299, PMID:34491895, PMID:31780330, PMID:17062563]. CRL3 activity is positively regulated by NEDD8 conjugation to CUL3 and negatively regulated by COP9 signalosome-mediated deneddylation; cycling between these states is essential for sustained ligase function and CUL3 protein stability [PMID:12781129, PMID:16127432]. Disease-causing mutations in CUL3 or its adaptors KLHL3 and KLHL7 disrupt CRL3 complex assembly or substrate ubiquitination, causing familial hyperkalemic hypertension (pseudohypoaldosteronism type II) and autosomal-dominant retinitis pigmentosa, respectively [PMID:23387299, PMID:21828050, PMID:34878901].

DDX23 (PRP28) is a DEAD-box RNA helicase central to pre-mRNA splicing, whose ATPase activity drives displacement of U1 snRNP from the 5' splice site and stable integration of the U4/U6-U5 tri-snRNP into the spliceosomal B complex [PMID:27377154, PMID:34035302]. The isolated protein adopts an autoinhibited conformation with an occluded ATP-binding site that is relieved only within the assembled spliceosome; its RS-like N-terminal domain, phosphorylated by SRPK2, mediates tri-snRNP association and direct interaction with the SR protein SRSF1 [PMID:24914973, PMID:18425142, PMID:38743621]. Beyond canonical splicing, DDX23 suppresses R-loops at transcription-stalled loci via Pol κ–mediated recruitment, promotes Drosha-dependent pri-miRNA processing, and functions as a nuclear dsRNA sensor that translocates to the cytoplasm upon viral infection to activate TRIF/MAVS-dependent innate immune signaling [PMID:28076779, PMID:41949541, PMID:26121981, PMID:31620127]. DDX23 also facilitates lncRNA-guided splicing of specific pre-mRNAs and regulates alternative splicing events including oncogenic FOXM1C isoform production [PMID:41360761, PMID:34966670].

hnRNP A1 is a multifunctional RNA- and DNA-binding protein that acts as a major regulator of alternative splicing, telomere maintenance, miRNA biogenesis, and IRES-dependent translation. Its two N-terminal RRMs form an antiparallel bipartite RNA-binding domain that binds high-affinity splicing silencer elements and then spreads cooperatively along RNA to antagonize SR protein binding and repress exon inclusion, while also allosterically remodeling pri-miRNA terminal loops to promote (pri-miR-18a) or inhibit (pri-let-7a) Drosha processing [PMID:11779509, PMID:29946118, PMID:20639884]. At telomeres, hnRNP A1 unfolds G-quadruplex structures via synergistic action of UP1 and its RGG-box and displaces RPA from single-stranded telomeric DNA in a TERRA-regulated manner to facilitate the RPA-to-POT1 switch and modulate telomerase access [PMID:16603717, PMID:21399625, PMID:30247678]. Nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling is governed by the M9/PY-NLS in the glycine-rich C-terminal domain and is regulated by an integrated network of post-translational modifications—including p38-mediated phosphorylation, S6K2-mediated phosphorylation, PRMT-mediated arginine methylation, SIRT1/6-mediated deacetylation, TRAF6-mediated ubiquitination, and O-GlcNAcylation—that couple signaling inputs to splicing, translation, and localization outputs; disease-associated mutations in the prion-like domain accelerate amyloid fibril formation nucleated at condensate interfaces, with the PY-NLS itself forming the fibril core [PMID:10769024, PMID:25324306, PMID:23455423, PMID:33311513, PMID:37749234].

KCTD10 is a substrate-recognition adaptor of the CUL3-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase complex that targets a broad range of substrates—including RhoB, SLC7A11, EIF3D, KCTD13, β-catenin, Notch1, and TCEA2—for ubiquitin-dependent degradation via K48, K63, or K27 linkage-specific polyubiquitination, thereby governing processes spanning endothelial barrier integrity, ferroptosis resistance, cortical neurogenesis, cardiac morphogenesis, and genome stability [PMID:29358211, PMID:38959043, PMID:38489388, PMID:25401743, PMID:40873559, PMID:41062692]. KCTD10 senses co-directional transcription–replication conflicts through bivalent binding to both the replisome and RNA polymerase machinery, recruiting CUL3 to ubiquitinate the elongation factor TCEA2 and permit replisome bypass; its loss causes TCEA2 retention and DNA damage accumulation [PMID:41062692]. KCTD10 undergoes liquid–liquid phase separation via its intrinsically disordered region, concentrating CUL3 activity at postsynaptic sites to degrade RhoB; a schizophrenia-associated p.C124W variant disrupts this phase separation, causing RhoB accumulation and synaptic defects [PMID:39565307]. In zebrafish, Kctd10 directly binds and represses the transcription factor Tbx5a to restrict atrioventricular canal identity, and Kctd10-null mice die at ~E10.5 with severe cardiovascular defects linked to Notch1 pathway dysregulation [PMID:24430697, PMID:25401743].

MARK2 (Par-1b/EMK1) is a serine/threonine kinase that serves as a master regulator of cell polarity, coordinating microtubule dynamics, actomyosin contractility, and vesicle trafficking in epithelia, neurons, and migrating cells. It is activated by LKB1-mediated T-loop phosphorylation and GSK-3β phosphorylation at Ser-212, and negatively regulated by aPKC phosphorylation at T595, which promotes 14-3-3 binding and cytoplasmic retention away from the plasma membrane; an intramolecular auto-inhibitory mechanism through the C-terminal KA1 domain further restricts its activity [PMID:14976552, PMID:15084291, PMID:16257959, PMID:30814118]. MARK2 phosphorylates a diverse set of substrates—including MAPs (tau, MAP2), Rab11-FIP2, GEF-H1, IRSp53, myosin II RLC, and the kinesin KIF13B—to control epithelial apicobasal polarity, lumen positioning, E-cadherin-based adhesion, directed cell migration, axon specification, and Hippo pathway signaling [PMID:14981097, PMID:16775013, PMID:22072711, PMID:35594862, PMID:20194617, PMID:23940457]. MARK2 knockout mice exhibit impaired spatial learning and microglial priming, and the bacterial oncoprotein H. pylori CagA directly binds and inhibits MARK2 to disrupt epithelial junctions [PMID:17196307, PMID:30654821, PMID:18005242].

MPRIP is a multifunctional scaffold protein that spatially targets myosin light chain phosphatase (MLCP) to actomyosin stress fibers, thereby controlling myosin II phosphorylation, contractility, and cytoskeletal dynamics across diverse cell types. Its N-terminal region binds and bundles F-actin (Kd ~0.5 µM), while its C-terminal coiled-coil domain binds the myosin phosphatase targeting subunit MYPT1 and mediates oligomerization; loss of MPRIP displaces MYPT1 from stress fibers and increases myosin light chain phosphorylation, augmenting contractility [PMID:12732640, PMID:16257966, PMID:31347175]. MPRIP additionally inactivates RhoA through a GAP-like activity, is phosphorylated by PKG to enhance MLCP function, and is cleaved by caspases during apoptosis to generate a MYPT1-binding fragment that regulates bleb retraction through localized myosin dephosphorylation [PMID:15545284, PMID:23723008, PMID:40344468]. In the nucleus, MPRIP binds PIP2, forms phase-separated condensates via its intrinsically disordered region, and recruits Tyr1-phosphorylated RNA Polymerase II to PIP2-containing structures, regulating transcription elongation and RNAPII condensate dynamics [PMID:33918018, PMID:36979361].

NACA (α-NAC) is a dual-function protein that acts both as a ribosome-associated chaperone safeguarding nascent polypeptide targeting fidelity and as a phosphorylation-regulated transcriptional coactivator. As a subunit of the nascent polypeptide-associated complex (NAC), NACA binds emerging nascent chains and prevents inappropriate SRP-dependent translocation of signal-peptide-lacking proteins into the ER [PMID:8047162]. ILK-mediated phosphorylation on Ser-43 triggers nuclear translocation of NACA, where it occupies promoters of osteocalcin and α1(I) collagen to coactivate c-Jun/AP-1-dependent transcription essential for osteoblast maturation and bone matrix composition, while GSK3β phosphorylation on Thr-159 opposes this by directing NACA for proteasomal degradation [PMID:15299025, PMID:15005626, PMID:19884350]. The crystal structure of the NAC dimerization domain reveals a nucleic acid-binding surface on α-NAC that is occluded by the β-NAC subunit in the heterodimer, providing a structural basis for how heterodimerization gates the transcriptional coactivator function [PMID:20214399].

NAE1 (APP-BP1) is the regulatory subunit of the heterodimeric NEDD8-activating E1 enzyme (NAE1–UBA3) that catalyzes the first step in the neddylation cascade, a post-translational modification pathway essential for cullin-RING ligase activation, cell cycle progression, meiotic recombination, neuromuscular junction formation, and immune cell function. NAE1 functions primarily as a scaffold that accelerates UBA3-catalyzed NEDD8 adenylation and thioester transfer to the E2 conjugating enzyme Ubc12, with substrate selectivity enforced by a conserved arginine gate in the heterodimer and the Ala72 residue of NEDD8 [PMID:14690597, PMID:12740388, PMID:29973603]. Post-translational regulation of NAE1 includes TRIP12-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of the free monomer, and K238 crotonylation that enhances neddylation activity toward substrates such as gelsolin, linking NAE1 to pathological cardiac hypertrophy [PMID:18627766, PMID:39229723]. Bi-allelic loss-of-function variants in NAE1 cause a human developmental disorder with impaired NF-κB signaling, lymphocyte activation defects, and skeletal abnormalities [PMID:36608681].

NEDD8 is a ubiquitin-like modifier whose conjugation to target proteins (neddylation) is a central regulatory switch for cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase (CRL) activity, proteotoxic stress responses, and apoptotic signaling. NEDD8 is activated by the heterodimeric E1 enzyme APPBP1–UBA3, transferred to dedicated E2 enzymes (UBE2M or UBE2F) that pair with distinct RING subunits (RBX1 or RBX2), and ligated to a conserved lysine on all cullin family members, inducing a dramatic conformational rearrangement of the cullin WHB domain and RBX1 RING that displaces the inhibitor CAND1, repositions the ubiquitin-loaded E2, and activates CRL-mediated substrate ubiquitination essential for cell-cycle progression, NF-κB signaling, and DNA replication licensing [PMID:9694792, PMID:10921923, PMID:18805092, PMID:19250909]. Beyond cullins, NEDD8 is conjugated to non-cullin substrates—including p53, p73, EGFR, caspases, and Smurf1—by E3 ligases such as Mdm2, c-Cbl, and IAPs, modulating their transcriptional activity, trafficking, or catalytic function, and these modifications are reversed by the deNEDDylases NEDP1/SENP8 and the COP9 signalosome [PMID:15242646, PMID:21145488, PMID:24821572, PMID:28475037]. Free, unanchored NEDD8 chains (linked through K11, K22, K48, or K60) and phospho-NEDD8 (S65) serve non-cullin functions: NEDD8 trimers inhibit PARP-1 via its zinc-finger domain, mono-NEDD8 and phospho-NEDD8 stimulate HSP70 ATPase activity to promote APAF1-dependent apoptosis, and under proteotoxic stress the ubiquitin E1 (UBE1) mediates atypical neddylation generating mixed NEDD8–ubiquitin and NEDD8–SUMO-2 chains on ribosomal and proteasomal substrates [PMID:30804002, PMID:31577950, PMID:34642328, PMID:33472076].

ORC2 is a core subunit of the origin recognition complex (ORC) that functions in DNA replication licensing, centromere maintenance, and replication-independent chromatin organization. ORC2 binds chromatin before S phase via its winged-helix domain in a cell-cycle-regulated manner controlled by CDK phosphorylation at Thr-116/Thr-226 (promoting dissociation) and PP1 dephosphorylation (promoting loading), with Orc1 required for initial ORC-(2–5) chromatin loading [PMID:8552193, PMID:22334659, PMID:24732362, PMID:16762929]. At centromeres, PIAS4-mediated SUMO2 modification of ORC2 recruits the demethylase KDM5A to maintain H3K4me2 levels, and loss of this SUMOylation causes heterochromatin re-replication, DNA damage, and polyploidy [PMID:27052177, PMID:29050267]. Beyond replication, DNA-bound ORC2 independently regulates chromatin compaction, repressive and activating histone marks, and CTCF-dependent chromatin loop formation at numerous genomic loci, while under replication stress Plk1 phosphorylates ORC2 at Ser188 to maintain pre-replicative complex integrity [PMID:40504688, PMID:21947279].

PPP1CB encodes the β catalytic subunit of protein phosphatase 1 (PP1cβ), a serine/threonine phosphatase that assembles into substrate-specific holoenzymes through regulatory subunits and dephosphorylates diverse targets including myosin regulatory light chain, PLK1, RAF1 (Ser259), p-STAT3, and tau, thereby controlling smooth muscle contraction, mitotic checkpoint signaling, RAS/MAPK pathway output, and neuronal phospho-tau homeostasis [PMID:30185619, PMID:29262732, PMID:30368668, PMID:39119928, PMID:16262633]. Regulatory subunit competition governs holoenzyme composition: MYPT1 targets PP1cβ to myosin for contractile regulation, while TIMAP competitively displaces MYPT1 and occludes the PP1cβ active site to inhibit myosin phosphatase activity in endothelial cells, and TRIP12-mediated ubiquitination degrades PP1cβ to relieve dephosphorylation of NF-κB pathway components [PMID:31315927, PMID:39155295]. De novo gain-of-function missense mutations in PPP1CB (e.g., Pro49Arg, Ala56Pro) cause a Noonan syndrome–like RASopathy with loose anagen hair [PMID:27264673, PMID:27681385]. Loss of PPP1CB phosphatase activity—via a recurrent YPEL5–PPP1CB chimeric transcript in chronic lymphocytic leukemia or via siRNA silencing—promotes leukemic cell proliferation, establishing PP1cβ as a growth-suppressive phosphatase in B-cell malignancy [PMID:23382248].

PPP1R12A (MYPT1) is the regulatory/targeting subunit of myosin light chain phosphatase (MLCP), assembling with PP1cβ through an intrinsically disordered N-terminal region that folds into an α-helix upon PP1 binding, and directing the holoenzyme toward myosin and additional substrates including EZH2, JMJD1A, and PLK1 to coordinate actomyosin contractility, cell migration, cytokinesis, centrosome maturation, and chromatin regulation [PMID:21142030, PMID:24712327, PMID:22641346, PMID:35293697]. MYPT1 activity is governed by an elaborate multisite phosphorylation code: ROCK-mediated phosphorylation at Thr696 autoinhibits the PP1 active site while Thr853 phosphorylation promotes MYPT1 dissociation from myosin, and PKG/PKA phosphorylation at Ser695/Ser668 sterically blocks ROCK access to Thr696, enabling NO/cGMP-mediated smooth muscle relaxation; cell-cycle kinases (CDK1, LATS1, Chk1, Chk2) phosphorylate distinct sites to control PLK1 inactivation and centrosome dynamics [PMID:10579722, PMID:15194681, PMID:24712327, PMID:22641346, PMID:31416392]. Non-phosphorylation modifications—O-GlcNAcylation that antagonizes inhibitory phosphorylation, SETD7-mediated methylation at Lys442 that stabilizes MYPT1 protein against proteasomal degradation, SIAH2-directed ubiquitination, and FIH-catalyzed asparagine hydroxylation—provide additional regulatory layers [PMID:32929277, PMID:21115810, PMID:19744480, PMID:19245366]. De novo loss-of-function variants in PPP1R12A cause a congenital syndrome (GUBS) affecting brain and urogenital development, consistent with essential roles in morphogenetic cell movements demonstrated by embryonic lethality in knockout mice and zebrafish [PMID:31883643, PMID:16145842, PMID:18776143].

RBX1 (ROC1) is the RING-H2 finger protein that serves as the catalytic subunit of cullin-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase (CRL) complexes, directly recruiting and activating E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes to catalyze polyubiquitin chain formation on a broad range of substrates including IκBα, p27, CDT1, Nrf2, Cyclin E, EXO1, and others, thereby governing cell cycle progression, NF-κB signaling, DNA damage responses, and antioxidant defense [PMID:10213691, PMID:10230406, PMID:21115485, PMID:29358211]. RBX1 binds the C-terminal cullin domain of multiple cullins (CUL1–5) through an intermolecular β-sheet to form a two-subunit catalytic core, with its isolated RING domain sufficient to activate E2 enzymes such as CDC34 and UBC5 for ubiquitin chain assembly [PMID:11961546, PMID:11861641, PMID:10230407]. RBX1 also functions as a NEDD8-E3 ligase that recruits UBC12 to promote cullin neddylation—a modification that markedly enhances CRL ubiquitin ligase activity—and its RING domain is the target of regulatory inputs including inhibition by Glomulin (which occludes the E2-binding surface), arsenite binding, and MAGE-C2 binding, as well as stabilization by USP15-mediated deubiquitination [PMID:12565873, PMID:10921923, PMID:22748924, PMID:29658272, PMID:16005295]. RBX1 is essential for mouse embryonic development, with knockout lethality partially rescued by co-deletion of the CRL substrate p27, and Treg-specific deletion causes fatal inflammatory disease linked to disrupted effector Treg homeostasis [PMID:19325126, PMID:35641500].

SART3 is a multifunctional nuclear RNA-binding protein that serves as the central recycling factor for U4/U6 di-snRNP reassembly after each round of pre-mRNA splicing. Its C-terminal RRMs bind U6 snRNA while its N-terminal HAT/TPR repeats interact with the U4/U6-specific 90K protein to bridge the two snRNAs; LSm2-8 proteins synergistically recruit SART3 to the 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate-bearing U6, and the HAT domain directs U6 snRNPs to Cajal bodies for assembly, with SART3 monitoring tri-snRNP maturation and sequestering incomplete intermediates [PMID:12032085, PMID:15314151, PMID:18567812, PMID:12578909, PMID:25600876]. Beyond splicing, SART3 functions as a histone chaperone that presents ubiquitinated H2B to USP15 for deubiquitination, serves as a nuclear import adaptor for USP4/USP15 via its bipartite NLS bound to importin-α, and promotes UV-damage tolerance by homodimerizing to bridge Polη and RAD18 for PCNA monoubiquitination at stalled replication forks [PMID:24526689, PMID:27060135, PMID:29590477]. SART3 also participates in gene regulation by binding pre-miR-34a to facilitate its biogenesis, interacting with HIV-1 Tat to potentiate LTR transactivation, suppressing androgen receptor transcriptional activity, and reciprocally regulating CMYC expression to control hematopoietic progenitor cell homeostasis [PMID:31619517, PMID:11959860, PMID:15031286, PMID:21447833].

SF1 functions both as a pre-mRNA splicing factor (SF1/mBBP/ZFM1) that recognizes intron branchpoint sequences and as a nuclear receptor transcription factor (NR5A1/SF-1) essential for steroidogenic tissue and hypothalamic development. As a splicing factor, SF1 binds the branchpoint sequence UACUAAC via its KH domain and zinc knuckle, cooperatively associates with U2AF65 to nucleate early spliceosome (E/commitment complex) formation, and recruits U2 snRNP through SURP domain interactions; this cooperative binding is positively regulated by KIS phosphorylation of the SPSP motif and negatively regulated by PKG-I phosphorylation at Ser20 [PMID:9182766, PMID:9512519, PMID:26420826, PMID:16420481, PMID:10449420]. SF1 additionally acts as a transcriptional repressor of activated transcription through interactions with EWS-family proteins and the elongation factor CA150 [PMID:9506990, PMID:11604498]. As the nuclear receptor NR5A1, SF-1 is essential for gonadotrope LH/FSH expression, adrenal cortex regression (regulated by SUMOylation-dependent Dax1 recruitment), and terminal differentiation of ventromedial hypothalamic neurons including BDNF transcription; its expression is controlled by WT1 and FOXL2 binding at the Sf1 promoter and its target gene selectivity is modulated by Wnt/β-catenin signaling [PMID:11124111, PMID:28893949, PMID:12727442, PMID:27888191, PMID:22128028].

SNRNP27 is a tri-snRNP-specific SR-related protein that functions within the human U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP spliceosomal complex, contributing to protein–protein interactions required for tri-snRNP integration into the spliceosome. It possesses an N-terminal SR domain with high similarity to the SR domain of U1-70K but lacks an RNA-binding domain, and it is phosphorylated both in vitro by the snRNP-associated protein kinase and in vivo in human cells [PMID:9085842, PMID:17081983]. Systematic interaction mapping and cryo-EM structural studies place SNRNP27 within the tri-snRNP protein–protein interaction network alongside core U5 and interface proteins such as hPrp8, hBrr2, hSnu114, hPrp6, and hSnu66 [PMID:16723661, PMID:30975767]. Assembly of SNRNP27 into U5/tri-snRNP particles is assisted by the R2TP/Prefoldin-like cochaperone complex via ZNHIT2 [PMID:28561026].

TDP-43 is a predominantly nuclear RNA- and DNA-binding protein that functions as a master regulator of RNA processing, controlling alternative splicing — particularly repression of cryptic exons in transcripts such as UNC13A and CFTR — mRNA stability, alternative polyadenylation, and mRNA transport to neurites, all through its two RRM domains that recognize UG-rich and G-quadruplex RNA sequences [PMID:11470789, PMID:26250685, PMID:35197626, PMID:26915990]. TDP-43 undergoes liquid–liquid phase separation via a transiently α-helical low-complexity C-terminal domain, and this condensation capacity is required for efficient binding at long UG-rich clusters, autoregulation through its own 3′UTR, and normal splicing function; ALS-linked mutations and post-translational modifications (CK1/CK2 phosphorylation, RRM acetylation, K136 SUMOylation) alter phase-separation dynamics, RNA-binding competence, and aggregation propensity [PMID:34380047, PMID:27545621, PMID:35112738, PMID:25556531, PMID:34390468]. Pathologically, cytoplasmic mislocalization of TDP-43 — driven by nucleocytoplasmic transport disruption, caspase-4-mediated cleavage, and stress-granule-mediated up-concentration coupled with oxidative stress — produces neurotoxic C-terminal fragments and amyloid filaments whose seeding requires proteolytic exposure of a buried β-sheet core, while mitochondrial TDP-43 impairs complex I and triggers cGAS–STING neuroinflammation via mtDNA release [PMID:18305110, PMID:30810811, PMID:40412392, PMID:37248338, PMID:33031745]. Dominant missense mutations in the TARDBP glycine-rich C-terminal domain cause familial and sporadic ALS and FTLD, and TDP-43 proteinopathy — characterized by hyperphosphorylated, ubiquitinated, cleaved cytoplasmic inclusions — is the defining pathological hallmark of these disorders [PMID:17023659, PMID:18309045].

THOC3 (Tex1) is a stoichiometric subunit of the THO complex, which together with Aly and UAP56 forms the conserved TREX (Transcription-EXport) complex that couples mRNA processing to nuclear export [PMID:11979277, PMID:23222130]. In human cells, THOC3-containing THO associates with spliced mRNA in a cap- and splicing-dependent manner, localizes to nuclear speckles, and is recruited near the 5′ end of transcripts to facilitate 5′-to-3′ export through the nuclear pore [PMID:15998806, PMID:17190602]. RNAi depletion studies demonstrate that THO and Aly are mutually required for association with spliced mRNA and for recruitment of UAP56, establishing THOC3 as integral to TREX assembly and bulk mRNA export [PMID:23222130]. In lung cancer cells, THOC3 additionally partners with YBX1 to promote transcription and cytoplasmic export of specific target mRNAs such as PFKFB4, linking its mRNA export function to glycolytic reprogramming and cell proliferation [PMID:37500615].

UBA3 is the catalytic subunit of the heterodimeric NEDD8-activating enzyme (NAE/E1), central to the neddylation pathway that regulates cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase activity and downstream protein degradation. UBA3 alone is sufficient for NEDD8 adenylation and thioester bond formation via a pseudo-ordered kinetic mechanism (ATP binds first, NEDD8 second), while its partner APPBP1 serves as a non-catalytic scaffold that accelerates the reaction rate [PMID:12740388, PMID:29973603]. A conserved arginine residue in the APPBP1–UBA3 complex acts as a selectivity gate that prevents misactivation of ubiquitin, and Ala72 of NEDD8 is a critical specificity determinant for E1 recognition [PMID:14690597, PMID:12740388]. The C-terminal ubiquitin-like β-grasp domain of UBA3 constitutes the E2 (Ubc12)-binding site, undergoing a conformational transition from a dynamic state to a kinked α-helix upon E2 engagement to enable NEDD8 transfer [PMID:22821745].

UBE2M (Ubc12) is the principal NEDD8-conjugating E2 enzyme that, through its catalytic Cys111, transfers NEDD8 to cullin substrates (CUL1–CUL4) to activate cullin-RING ligase (CRL) complexes, thereby governing protein turnover central to cell-cycle control, DNA damage repair, immune homeostasis, and metabolic signaling [PMID:10828074, PMID:25025768, PMID:35641500]. UBE2M is recruited by the NEDD8 E1 (APPBP1–UBA3) via a ubiquitin-fold domain on the E1, and its selectivity toward CUL3 is enhanced by the co-E3 factor DCN1, which engages UBE2M's N-terminal peptide [PMID:15694336, PMID:29074978, PMID:29438612]. Beyond cullins, UBE2M neddylates non-cullin substrates including TRIM21, MKK7, USP39, and NEDD4, thereby regulating inflammatory cytokine production, JNK signaling, cell-cycle progression, and fatty acid metabolism [PMID:37343564, PMID:41361309, PMID:41680469, PMID:40744915]. Under stress conditions UBE2M can also function as a ubiquitylation E2 within the Parkin–DJ-1 complex to degrade UBE2F and inactivate CRL5, and its own abundance is controlled by HIF-1/AP-1 transcription and TRIM21-mediated ubiquitination [PMID:29932898, PMID:36662617].

UBTF encodes an architectural multi-HMG-box transcription factor (UBF) that is the principal organizer of ribosomal DNA chromatin and a master regulator of RNA polymerase I transcription. UBF dimerizes through its N-terminal domain, bends ~140 bp of DNA into a superhelical loop (the enhancesome), and binds across the entire rDNA repeat to maintain nucleosome-free, transcriptionally competent chromatin; its cellular levels directly determine the number of active rRNA gene copies, and its depletion causes histone H1-dependent gene silencing, nucleolar disassembly, and early embryonic lethality [PMID:19103806, PMID:27614293, PMID:11756560]. At the rDNA promoter, phosphorylation-dependent interaction of UBF's C-terminal activation domain with SL1 and of its HMG boxes with the Pol I subunit PAF53 enables pre-initiation complex assembly and promoter escape; these interactions are regulated by CK2, CDK4/cyclin D1, CDK2/cyclin E/A, ERK1/2, and PKCι phosphorylation at distinct sites, as well as by CBP-mediated acetylation and ESET-mediated methylation, integrating growth-factor, cell-cycle, and mTOR signaling into rRNA output [PMID:10202152, PMID:11698641, PMID:11741541, PMID:16971462, PMID:32350115, PMID:11106745, PMID:24234436]. Beyond rDNA, UBTF occupies highly expressed Pol II gene loci including histone gene clusters, where its depletion causes DNA damage and genomic instability; the recurrent de novo E210K gain-of-function variant causes childhood-onset neurodegeneration through enhanced rDNA promoter binding and dysregulated rRNA metabolism, while UBTF tandem duplications drive acute myeloid leukemia by mislocalizing UBTF to HOX/MEIS1 loci [PMID:25452314, PMID:28777933, PMID:37890156].

ZC3H8 (Fliz1) is a CCCH-type zinc finger protein that functions as a transcriptional repressor and a component of the Little Elongation Complex (LEC) involved in snRNA transcription. It represses GATA-3 transcription by binding a negative cis-acting element in the GATA-3 first intron [PMID:12077251], and in zebrafish a loss-of-function mutation causes digestive organ degeneration through derepression of NF-κB-mediated inflammatory signaling, rescued by NF-κB pathway inhibition [PMID:29871925]. ZC3H8 localizes to PML bodies and Cajal bodies, where CK2-mediated phosphorylation of a conserved N-terminal threonine regulates nuclear body foci number, and its expression promotes oncogenic phenotypes including proliferation, migration, and tumor formation in mammary cells [PMID:30041613]. ZC3H8 transcript levels depend on SCNM1-mediated minor (U12) intron splicing, as demonstrated by SCNM1 knockout and rescue experiments [PMID:36084634].
